distillation_scope: Pure disease-name first-layer leaf distillation for Familial Mediterranean fever. This leaf models the full clinical manifold of FMF without adding subtype, genotype, trigger, ethnicity, amyloidosis, or attack-pattern qualifiers to the disease name.

latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: MEFV/pyrin pathway dysregulation lowers the threshold for innate inflammasome activation and recurrent neutrophilic inflammation.

The disease expresses as short self-limited inflammatory attacks separated by relatively well intervals; attacks may be triggered by physiologic stress, infection, menstruation, exertion, or no clear trigger.
IL-1 beta amplification and neutrophil recruitment drive fever, leukocytosis, high CRP/SAA, fibrinogen, reactive thrombocytosis, and pain during attacks.
Sterile peritoneal and mesenteric serositis produces recurrent acute abdomen, guarding, nausea/vomiting, ascites, and surgical mimic presentations.
Sterile pleural and pericardial inflammation causes pleuritic chest pain, pleural or pericardial effusion, transient pulmonary inflammatory opacities, and rare hemodynamic compromise.
Attack-related neutrophilic inflammation can involve synovium, periarticular tissues, muscles, scrotal tunics, and skin, including monoarthritis and erysipelas-like erythema.
Repeated or persistent serum amyloid A elevation creates risk for AA amyloid deposition, especially in kidney, when inflammation is undertreated or genetically severe.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Renal AA amyloid organ damage activity
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Renal AA amyloid deposition produces proteinuria, nephrotic syndrome, hypoalbuminemia, edema, progressive kidney failure, dialysis need, and rare adrenal or systemic amyloid complications.

mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Pyrin dysregulation creates the disease's recurrent attack tendency.
Attack gating rapidly amplifies IL-1 beta and neutrophilic acute-phase inflammation.
Peritoneal attacks are the most frequent serositis expression of FMF.
Pleural and pericardial attacks are short sterile serositis episodes.
FMF attacks may localize to joints, muscles, skin, or scrotal serosa.
Sustained or repeatedly high SAA from active inflammation drives AA amyloidogenesis over time.
Renal AA amyloid deposition is the dominant severe organ complication of uncontrolled FMF.
The history of recurrent brief febrile attacks is a clinical expression of the attack gate.
Repeated short attacks of abdominal, chest, joint, or serosal pain are a high-specificity presentation pattern.
FMF attacks commonly last hours to a few days rather than weeks.
IL-1 beta acute-phase activity raises temperature during attacks.
Fever history captures attacks even when afebrile at a single snapshot.
CRP rises strongly during inflammatory attacks.
SAA is a sensitive acute-phase marker and the substrate for AA amyloid risk.
Neutrophilic inflammation produces leukocytosis in many attacks.
Neutrophils dominate the acute inflammatory response.
ESR rises with acute-phase proteins and inflammation.
Reactive thrombocytosis may accompany acute or persistent inflammation.
Fibrinogen is an acute-phase protein and can be markedly elevated.
Fever, pain, and inflammation often produce tachycardia.
Sterile peritonitis causes severe abdominal pain.
Guarding and peritoneal signs can mimic a surgical abdomen.
Peritoneal inflammation and pain can cause nausea or vomiting.
Sterile peritoneal inflammation or nephrotic physiology can produce ascites.
Pleural serositis causes pleuritic chest pain.
Pericardial or pleural attacks may present as anterior chest pain.
Pleural inflammation can cause small to moderate effusions.
Pericardial inflammation can produce pericardial effusion.
Pericarditis is uncommon but recognized in FMF.
Transient inflammatory pulmonary opacities can accompany pleuropericardial FMF attacks and mimic infection.
FMF can cause acute monoarthritis or oligoarthritis, often lower-extremity predominant.
Joint pain may occur with or without objective arthritis.
Myalgia and exertional leg pain occur in FMF.
Erysipelas-like erythema around lower limbs is a characteristic but not universal FMF skin finding.
Scrotal or tunica vaginalis inflammation can occur during pediatric FMF attacks.
Longstanding SAA elevation drives AA amyloid deposition.
Renal amyloid commonly presents with proteinuria.
Quantified urine protein rises into nephrotic range when renal amyloid is severe.
Heavy proteinuria, edema, and hypoalbuminemia define nephrotic presentation.
Nephrotic urinary protein loss lowers serum albumin.
Hypoalbuminemia and renal salt/water retention cause edema.
Progressive renal amyloid can cause chronic kidney failure.
Untreated renal amyloidosis can progress to ESKD.
Systemic amyloid can rarely involve adrenal glands.
Ordinary attacks have low mortality, but severe serositis, dehydration, or diagnostic delay can increase acute risk.
Advanced renal or systemic amyloidosis is the dominant driver of FMF-related mortality.

axes.shape_free_text: History of repeated self-limited fever episodes, often lasting hours to a few days with well intervals.
Recurrent short attacks involving peritoneal, pleural, pericardial, synovial, skin, or scrotal serosal inflammation.
Duration of a typical attack; FMF classically clusters around short attacks but atypical or complicated courses can be longer.
Measured body temperature during an attack.
Reported fever burden across current or prior attacks.
Heart rate during pain, fever, or serositis.
Respiratory rate; may rise with fever, pain, pleuritis, or pulmonary involvement.
Oxygen saturation; usually preserved but may fall with pleural, pulmonary, or pericardial complications.
Mean arterial pressure; usually normal unless dehydration, sepsis mimic, adrenal insufficiency, or advanced organ failure coexist.
Abdominal pain from sterile peritonitis, mesenteric inflammation, or nephrotic/amyloid complications.
Guarding, rebound, peritoneal tenderness, or surgical-abdomen mimic from sterile peritoneal serositis.
Nausea or vomiting during abdominal attacks.
Ascites from peritoneal inflammation or nephrotic hypoalbuminemia.
Pleuritic chest pain during pleural serositis attacks.
Anterior or nonspecific chest pain from pleural or pericardial attack physiology.
Pleural effusion from pleural serositis, usually small but can be clinically relevant.
Pericardial effusion from pericardial serositis.
Clinical or imaging-supported pericardial inflammation in FMF.
Transient noninfectious pulmonary infiltrates or ground-glass/consolidative opacities accompanying pleuropericardial FMF attacks; uncommon and a pneumonia mimic.
Dyspnea during pleural, pericardial, pulmonary, or severe systemic attacks.
Acute inflammatory arthritis, often monoarticular or oligoarticular and lower-extremity predominant.
Joint pain during musculoskeletal FMF attacks.
Myalgia or exertional leg pain during FMF attacks.
Erysipelas-like erythema, classically lower-leg or ankle-region painful erythema.
Scrotal swelling or tunica vaginalis inflammation during FMF, more often pediatric.
Peripheral, pretibial, generalized, or nephrotic edema from renal amyloidosis or severe hypoalbuminemia.
Splenomegaly from chronic inflammation, amyloidosis, or reactive systemic disease.
C-reactive protein during attack or persistent subclinical inflammation.
Serum amyloid A acute-phase concentration; can be extremely high during attacks and persistent elevation drives AA amyloid risk.
ESR during attack or chronic inflammation.
Peripheral leukocyte count during attack.
Absolute neutrophil count during attack.
Hemoglobin; may be normal during isolated attacks or low with chronic inflammation/renal disease.
Platelet count; can rise reactively with inflammation.
Fibrinogen as an acute-phase protein.
Serum albumin; falls with nephrotic protein loss and inflammation.
Serum creatinine; usually normal in uncomplicated attacks and elevated with renal amyloidosis or kidney failure.
Blood urea nitrogen; rises with renal amyloidosis, dehydration, or kidney failure.
Detectable proteinuria, especially from renal AA amyloid.
Quantified 24-hour urine protein; nephrotic-range values are common with renal amyloidosis.
Composite nephrotic presentation with heavy proteinuria, hypoalbuminemia, edema, and often hyperlipidemia.
Daily hazard of clinically meaningful AA amyloid deposition from persistent SAA exposure.
Daily hazard of progression to end-stage kidney disease from renal amyloidosis or severe chronic renal damage.
Daily hazard of clinically significant adrenal amyloid involvement; rare systemic amyloidosis complication.
Host context that limits colchicine use, including intolerance, severe diarrhea, cytopenia, myopathy risk, interacting drugs, or advanced renal/hepatic impairment.
Need to adjust colchicine or other medications for kidney function and drug interactions.
Concurrent serious infection context that changes the safety of IL-1 blockade or immunosuppression.

Lifespan outcome hazard for FMF, usually low in controlled disease but rising with severe untreated inflammation, renal AA amyloidosis, ESKD, systemic amyloidosis, dehydration, or severe cardiopulmonary serositis.

axis_couplings.clinical_rationale: Fever and CRP rise together during active attacks, though either can be muted at a single snapshot.
CRP and SAA are acute-phase reactants driven by the same inflammatory burst.
Peritoneal signs are the examination correlate of severe abdominal serositis.
Pleuritic pain and pleural effusion may co-occur during pleural attacks.
Pericardial inflammation commonly explains effusion when present.
Cumulative SAA exposure raises AA amyloid hazard.
Heavy proteinuria is central to nephrotic syndrome.
Sustained nephrotic renal amyloidosis increases kidney-failure hazard.
ESKD is a major downstream contributor to FMF mortality risk.

treatments.clinical_role: Long-term disease-modifying prophylaxis to reduce attacks, suppress SAA/CRP, and prevent AA amyloidosis; not a rapid analgesic for an attack already underway.

trajectory_modifications.clinical_rationale: Adherent colchicine reduces attack frequency and severity over days to weeks.
Colchicine suppresses neutrophilic inflammation and acute-phase activity.
SAA suppression is the prevention path for AA amyloidosis.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Intolerance, toxicity, or interacting drugs can prevent adequate dosing.
Advanced kidney disease raises colchicine toxicity risk and changes dosing.

treatments.clinical_role: Corrects undertreatment, nonadherence, underdosing, or avoidable interaction/toxicity issues before declaring colchicine resistance.

trajectory_modifications.clinical_rationale: Consistent exposure is required for prophylactic attack control.
Improved long-term inflammation control lowers amyloid hazard.

treatments.display_name: NSAIDs, paracetamol, and hydration during attacks
treatments.clinical_role: Symptomatic acute-attack support; it does not replace disease-modifying prophylaxis or prevent amyloidosis.

trajectory_modifications.clinical_rationale: Analgesics and hydration reduce perceived pain and dehydration physiology.
Antipyretics reduce fever without changing the long-term disease manifold.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: NSAIDs may be unsafe with advanced kidney disease or nephrotic complications.

treatments.clinical_role: IL-1 blockade for colchicine-resistant or colchicine-intolerant FMF and selected severe inflammatory complications.

trajectory_modifications.clinical_rationale: Anakinra directly blocks IL-1 signaling and can rapidly lower acute-phase activity.
IL-1 blockade can reduce SAA when colchicine is inadequate.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Active infection must be handled before or during IL-1 blockade decisions.

treatments.clinical_role: Longer-acting IL-1 beta blockade for colchicine-resistant or colchicine-intolerant FMF when sustained suppression is needed.

trajectory_modifications.clinical_rationale: Canakinumab suppresses IL-1 beta mediated acute-phase inflammation.
Sustained IL-1 beta blockade can reduce persistent SAA exposure.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Long-acting IL-1 beta blockade is risky when serious infection is active.

treatments.display_name: Renal amyloidosis, nephrotic, and CKD management
treatments.clinical_role: Nephrology management for proteinuria, nephrotic edema, blood pressure, kidney failure, dialysis, and transplant while inflammatory control is optimized.

trajectory_modifications.clinical_rationale: Diuresis, salt restriction, and nephrotic care reduce edema.
Kidney-protective management and renal replacement planning reduce complication hazard but do not erase amyloid biology.

treatments.display_name: Kidney replacement or transplant for FMF amyloidosis
treatments.clinical_role: Renal replacement therapy or transplantation for advanced FMF-related ESKD, paired with ongoing inflammation suppression to prevent recurrent amyloid.

trajectory_modifications.clinical_rationale: Renal replacement and transplant reduce uremic mortality risk in advanced kidney failure.

present.clinical_rationale: Turkish, Armenian, Arab, North African Jewish, Sephardic Jewish, and other Mediterranean ancestry contexts increase prior probability when the presentation is compatible.
Confirmed pathogenic MEFV context strongly supports the manifold, but case JSON should keep genetic testing confirmatory unless the runtime mode includes diagnostic workup evidence.
Some MEFV genotypes, especially severe exon 10 patterns, are associated with earlier onset, arthritis, amyloid risk, and lower colchicine response.
Repeated short self-resolving abdominal, chest, joint, or serosal attacks are the clinical pattern that distinguishes FMF from many one-time mimics.
FMF often begins in childhood; long diagnostic delay increases cumulative inflammatory exposure.
Missing or inadequate prophylaxis permits recurrent SAA elevation and amyloidosis.
Nephrotic or renal amyloid context reshapes the disease toward chronic renal complication axes.
Resistance or intolerance leaves residual inflammation and is the context for IL-1 blockade.

supportive_care.clinical_role: Document attack duration, interval, fever, serositis site, triggers, and well intervals while still evaluating acute abdomen, sepsis, pulmonary embolism, appendicitis, IBD, gynecologic disease, pericarditis, and infection when presentation warrants.
Trend CRP/SAA and check urinalysis or urine protein regularly because subclinical SAA elevation and proteinuria drive long-term amyloid risk.
FMF can mimic appendicitis or peritonitis; repeated negative imaging/cultures and short self-limited attacks support FMF, but peritoneal catastrophe must still be assessed on each presentation.
Use genetic counseling, family evaluation, and adherence education once diagnosis is established; do not let genetic labels substitute for observed clinical evidence in presentation-only ranking.
Coordinate nephrology care for proteinuria, nephrotic syndrome, renal amyloid, CKD, dialysis, transplant planning, and renal dosing.
Exclude or manage serious infection before IL-1 blockade when fever, infiltrates, effusions, or immunosuppression context makes infection plausible.

quality_notes: No first_line, preferred, guideline_recommended, or indication_strength labels are used.
Genotype, ethnicity, amyloidosis, and colchicine response are represented as risk/context/treatment mechanisms rather than disease-name qualifiers.
